title: MB9-26871
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): XXXX XXXX XXXX (Appellant), a citizen of Nigeria, appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejecting his claim for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX (Appellant), a citizen of Nigeria, appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejecting his claim for refugee protection.

The Appellant is of Yoruba ethnicity and is Christian. He fears harm at the hands of Sango idol worshippers in XXXX XXXX Lagos, because he refused to become the chief priest (or Abore) of the community. The Appellant alleges that he was attacked on several occasions for refusing to become the chief priest and that despite relocating twice within Nigeria, the perpetrators were able to locate him, threaten him, and attack him.

The RPD denied the Appellant's claim for refugee protection because it did not believe his allegations that he faced a risk of persecution or harm for refusing the worshippers' request to be chief priest. The RPD did not believe the Appellant's allegations because it found that the Appellant failed to provide reasonable explanations for contradictions, inconsistencies and omissions in his evidence and found that the documentary evidence did not support his allegations.

The Appellant argues that the RPD did not properly consider the explanations he provided with respect to the alleged issues in his testimony, and that the RPD did not properly consider the documentary evidence, including the objective country information.

I find that the RPD was correct in its assessment of the Appellant's claim. The Appellant is not credible in his allegations and the documentary evidence does not assist the Appellant in establishing his claim.
I dismiss the appeal. The RPD was correct in finding that the Appellant is neither a Convention1 refugee nor a person in need of protection.

My role is to look at all the evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision.2 While I find that the RPD erred in its consideration of one of the country condition documents, I conclude overall that the RPD was correct in its determination that the Appellant's allegations are not credible and that the documentary evidence does not overcome the credibility concerns. The Appellant has not established that he faces a serious possibility of persecution or that, on a balance of probabilities, he faces a risk to his life, a danger of torture, or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment if he returns to Nigeria. Country conditions documentation

The RPD erred in failing to consider the totality of the documentary evidence before drawing a conclusion on the objective basis for the Appellant's allegations of risk. The RPD considered the National Documentation Package (NDP) for Nigeria, dated August 20, 2019, which contains a 2010 Response to Information Request (RIR) relating to consequences for a person to refuse a chief priest or fetish priest position for which they have been selected in south and central Nigeria.3 The RPD relied on the statements of two professors quoted in the RIR that there would be no consequences for an individual who refused a position of chief priest. The RPD found that the Appellant failed to refute this evidence. The Appellant argues on appeal that the RPD relied on an excerpt of the research document without consideration of the document in its entirety. He argues that in doing so, the RPD imposed unwarranted expectations on him and failed to afford him the benefit of the doubt.

I agree with the Appellant that it was an error for the RPD to rely on the excerpt of the RIR without consideration of the contents of the document in its entirety. In addition to the statements relied on by the RPD, there are other opinions quoted in the RIR that suggests that some individuals may face consequences from Sango idol worshippers if the individual declines to take an inherited position. A Professor of Anthropology at Franklin & Marshall College stated that Christians have been refusing to take their inherited offices in shrines since the beginning of Christian missionization in Nigeria. However, the professor went on to state that "in the old days," if an individual did refuse to assume the inherited position as a shrine priest, the servants of the shrine might "force" the individual to assume the role and that even today, there are people who maintain their ties to indigenous religion who swear that the shrine deities will find a way to punish those who refuse this.4

A Professor of Anthropology at Southern Illinois University (SIU) stated that in many communities it would be considered "a big problem" if someone refused to take on the inherited role of shrine priest. The SIU Professor further said people would believe that the individual was inviting "divine wrath" on themselves, as well as on the local community.5

The evidence in the RIR is mixed as to whether individuals who refuse to accept a position of chief priest would face repercussions from other worshippers; however, the RPD only referred to the portion that contradicted the Appellant's testimony. While it was open to the RPD to reach its own conclusions about the objective basis for the risk, it was required to consider all of the relevant information before doing so. Where a decision-maker refers in some detail to evidence supporting its finding but is silent on evidence pointing to the opposite conclusion, it may be easier to infer that the decision-maker overlooked the contradictory evidence when making its finding of fact.6 Here, the RPD Reasons are silent with respect to the evidence that individuals may face repercussions for refusing to accept a position of chief priest, which leads me to conclude that this evidence was not considered.

Building on this position that the documentary evidence was conclusive that individuals who refuse to accept a position of chief priest would not face repercussions, the RPD also concluded that the Appellant was inconsistent about why he was being required to take on the role of chief priest. The RPD noted the Appellant's testimony that, like him, his mother and siblings were practicing Christians and none of them followed the Sango idol worship. He testified that he was identified specifically to become a Sango chief priest because his father was a chief priest and the Appellant, as the first-born son of his father, was required to take over the position from his father. I find that it was not inconsistent with the information in the RIR for some family members to be free to follow Christianity while the first-born son may be expected by those who follow the Sango idol worship to be expected to take on an inherited role.

Although I find that the RPD erred in its consideration of the RIR, I find that this error is not determinative of the appeal, as there remain a number of other findings of the RPD that are upheld on appeal relating directly to the credibility of the Appellant's evidence that he was targeted in order to become the next chief priest. Credibility

In reviewing the findings of the RPD and in reaching my own findings relating to credibility, I am mindful that there is a presumption of truthfulness when a claimant has sworn to the truth of their allegations unless there are valid reasons to doubt their truthfulness.7 Having reviewed the record in its entirety, including the transcript and audio recording of the RPD hearing, I find that the concerns identified by the RPD, including contradictions, inconsistencies, and omissions on key issues that have not been reasonably explained are sufficient to rebut the presumption that the Appellant was telling the truth. Lack of spontaneity, vague and evolving testimony

The RPD was correct to doubt the credibility of the Appellant's allegations due to a lack of spontaneity in the hearing and vague and evolving testimony. The RPD opened its credibility analysis with a finding that there were many reasons for doubting the truthfulness of the Appellant's testimony, namely that the Appellant was frequently not spontaneous in his responses, often failing to provide details when describing the attacks he had allegedly endured, and adjusting his testimony several times during the hearing. While the RPD does not dedicate much analysis in its decision to this general finding regarding the credibility of his testimony, focussing instead on specific issues that will be addressed below, a review of the transcript and audio recording of the hearing reveals many concerns that were raised by the RPD throughout the hearing where the Appellant was vague in his testimony, required prompting or follow up questions from the RPD, and where his testimony changed without reasonable explanation.

The Appellant argues that a lack of spontaneity is not a basis for a negative credibility finding and that a critical margin of appreciation was never applied by the RPD to perceived flaws in the testimony. I disagree with this argument for the following reasons. It is not the lack of spontaneity alone that raises a concern regarding the truthfulness of the Appellant's testimony, but the lack of spontaneity in conjunction with the contradictions and adjustments that arose upon further questioning, leading to a disjointedness and lack of coherency in the Appellant's testimony that negatively affects the credibility of his evidence.

For example, the Appellant's evidence was inconsistent regarding whether the threats and attacks against him started in 2011, 2012 or 2016. The Appellant stated in his narrative statement that accompanied his amended Basis of Claim (BOC) form that his problems started on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2011 when he refused to comply with the request of Sango idol worshippers to become the next Abore or chief priest. He stated that individuals started threatening his life, and on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2012 he reported all of the issues to police.

In testimony at the RPD hearing, the Appellant stated that it was XXXX 2016 when problems first started, and individuals were attacking him.8 He then stated that the first attack occurred on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2011 when he told the perpetrators that he was not interested in idol worship. He stated that he was attacked by XXXX XXXX XXXX,9 who is his uncle and the head of the family. When asked for more details, he stated that there were about five people who attacked him, but that he reported XXXX XXXX XXXX to the police. It is not clear from the Appellant's testimony whether he went to the police in both 2011 and 2012 or if he was referring only to the complaint filed in XXXX 2012 for which he had provided a police report. Although confronted by the RPD that he provided differing dates regarding when the problems and attacks started, the responses failed to fully clarify the timeline of events.

The Appellant's evidence regarding key details of the XXXX XXXX XXXX 2012 attack were also inconsistent. In his BOC form narrative, he states that XXXX XXXX XXXX was the suspect in the attack and does not mention any other assailants. In testimony before the RPD, he stated that there were four assailants with XXXX XXXX XXXX laying the first slap and the others following with punches. When asked by the RPD to describe the individuals, the Appellant first stated that the individuals were "elderly" then stated that they were "area boys."10 When confronted by the RPD on this discrepancy, he stated that they were elderly people but behaving like people with mental problems, so he viewed them to be area boys. Despite this attempted clarification, the Appellant later testified that his family who were witnessing the beating could do nothing to intervene because the individuals beating him were older than them. The Appellant testified that his wife's pleas for the assailants to stop were what allowed him to escape, which contradicted his statement that his family could do nothing to intervene. The Appellant responded that his family could not attack or retaliate against the assailants because of their age, but could only beg. While the response from the Appellant provides some clarification, it does not explain why the Appellant's testimony evolved in his description of the assailants or the responses of his family members. In this way, the Appellant's testimony was difficult to follow and raises concerns regarding the credibility of his statements.

The RPD specifically concluded that the Appellant provided inconsistent evidence regarding the number of individuals arrested for the XXXX XXXX XXXX 2012 attack. In his BOC form narrative, the Appellant states that XXXX XXXX XXXX was arrested. In the RPD hearing however, he stated that two errands boys were arrested, and that XXXX XXXX XXXX came to post bail for them. The RPD confronted the Appellant that the police report submitted in support of his claim states that XXXX XXXX XXXX was arrested. The Appellant then changed his testimony, stating that XXXX XXXX XXXX and his two boys were all arrested. The RPD asked the Appellant why he changed his testimony from stating that only the two errand boys were arrested and not XXXX XXXX XXXX. The Appellant responded that he said that all three were arrested. This explanation fails to acknowledge or explain the inconsistency in the Appellant's testimony.

The RPD asked the Appellant why the police report does not mention that two boys were also arrested along with XXXX XXXX XXXX. The Appellant responded that the report does state that XXXX XXXX XXXX was arrested with two suspects. On an independent review of the police report, it is evident that it refers only to the arrest of XXXX XXXX XXXX and does not indicate that any other individuals were arrested. The explanation for the discrepancy is not reasonable as it fails to acknowledge that there is a discrepancy between the Appellant's testimony and the police report.

The attacks by the Sango idol worshippers form the basis for the Appellant's refugee claim. It is reasonable to expect that he would be able to provide consistent evidence regarding the timeline of events and the details of an attack that led him to file a complaint with the police and led to arrests. When the inconsistencies were brought to the Appellant's attention, the Appellant did not offer reasonable explanations as to why his testimony was inconsistent, but rather would simply reiterate that his most recent statement was correct. The RPD was correct to find that the lack of spontaneity and vague and evolving testimony impugns the Appellant's credibility as to whether the threats and attacks occurred. Police Report
The RPD correctly concluded that the police report provided by the Appellant is not credible evidence and should be given no weight.

The RPD concluded that the police report was fraudulent because it had determined that the Appellant was not credible regarding the central allegation of risk that he was being threatened and had been attacked by XXXX XXXX XXXX. The RPD also noted the documentary evidence from the NDP that documentation fraud is highly prevalent in Nigeria. The Appellant argues that the RPD erred by not providing notice that the authenticity of the document was an issue.

The RPD was not relying on an extrinsic forensic assessment of the document to determine that it was fraudulent, but rather relied on the inconsistencies in the information in the report compared to the Appellant's testimony and the internal inconsistencies and the omissions by the Appellant that have impugned his credibility. The RPD brought these issues to the attention of the Appellant in the hearing and asked for a response.11 The Appellant responded that the report supports his position taken at the hearing that XXXX XXXX XXXX was arrested with two suspects. As mentioned earlier, on review of the report, it is evident that it refers only to the arrest of XXXX XXXX XXXX and does not indicate that any other individuals were arrested. I find that the RPD provided sufficient opportunity to the Appellant to respond to the issues with the police report but that the Appellant failed to reasonably explain the discrepancy.

The Appellant submits that a negative inference should not be drawn from the fact that the report is silent regarding two additional arrestees. I disagree. The police report is written in a letter form, addressed to the Deputy Commissioner of Police for Lagos State. It states that it is a police investigation report regarding the criminal complaint of threat to life reported by XXXX XXXXagainst XXXX XXXX XXXX. The report is detailed in its description of the initiating complaint and the investigation that followed. It documents that the investigation resulted in the arrest of XXXX XXXX XXXX and describes his release on bail with sureties, the subsequent absconding of XXXX XXXX XXXX, and the determination that he and his sureties were still at large. The report states that further investigation revealed that XXXX XXXX XXXX continues to threaten the Appellant and made an attempt on his life on a different occasion. The report states that the force is presently on the look out for XXXX XXXX XXXX and his sureties and that the case has been detailed for conclusion of investigation. The report concludes by indicating that it is for the deputy commission's information and directive.

Given the detailed nature of the report which appears to have been written to provide a comprehensive account of the investigation, it is reasonable to expect that if two additional people were arrested in connection with the incident, this would have been mentioned in the report. Given that the Appellant remains adamant that there were three individuals arrested, not one as indicated in the report, the report does not assist the Appellant in establishing that his version of events is true and therefore is given no weight. Omission of threats towards son

The Appellant did not declare in his BOC form that his son was approached and threatened by Sango idol worshippers. The RPD was correct to draw a negative inference from this omission. This was a significant and material omission as it speaks to the extent to which the Sango worshippers were pursuing the Appellant. The Appellant failed to provide a reasonable explanation for the omission. I find, as the RPD did, that the omission impacts the credibility of the Appellant's allegation that he and his son were pursued by the Sango worshippers.

At the RPD hearing, the Appellant stated that on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2014, his son was approached by members of Sango idol worshippers and told that if his father continued to refuse the position that he would have to become the next chief priest. He testified that they told his son that if he also refused, they would do the same to him as they did to the Appellant. He testified that the Sango worshippers continue to monitor his son. When asked why the Appellant did not declare this significant event in his BOC form, he stated that, "I did not put it because I was after my own life first."12

The RPD found that the explanation for the omission was unreasonable. It found that the allegation that the son was approached and threatened is significant because it speaks to the ongoing interest of the alleged agents of harm to have a chief priest in the community and that if the Sango worshippers truly had an interest in persecuting the Appellant and his son, it would be reasonable for the Appellant to include this allegation in his BOC form.

The Appellant argues that the failure to mention his son in his BOC form should not have been fatal given that the Appellant's response was reasonable. The Appellant argues that the explanation provided by the RPD is laconic. I disagree. The Appellant specifically mentioned in his BOC form narrative that he relocated to Ibadan on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2014 and that he left his family in Lagos. It is reasonable to expect that he would have also mentioned his son being confronted by Sango worshippers on that same day, if it had occurred, given that it is directly related to his central allegation. Additionally, continued efforts by his alleged persecutors to pressure him through threats and monitoring of his family members is directly related to his allegations. His response that he was after his own life first does not reasonably explain the omission when the targeting of family members, if true, supports his own claim. The Federal Court has held that all the important facts and details of a claim must be included in the BOC form and that failing to do so can affect the credibility of all or part of a claimant's testimony.13 The Court has also held that important omissions, contradictions and implausibilities regarding central allegations of the Applicant's claim can be dispositive of the claim.14 Lack of relocation of family

The RPD was correct to draw a negative inference on the Appellant's credibility from his failure to relocate his family in light of his allegation that his son was targeted by the Sango idol worshippers. The Appellant stated before the RPD that his son was not in as much danger as him, given that his son was still young and not yet of the age to be initiated as chief priest. He also stated that he could not relocate his family due to a lack of means to support them elsewhere.

The RPD found that the Appellant did not reasonably explain his lack of efforts to relocate his family and drew a negative inference on his credibility from what it deemed to be incompatible behaviour in leaving his family in XXXX if his son was being targeted. The RPD found that it was reasonable to expect the Appellant to take some kind of concrete measure to ensure his son's safety or to at least try to ask his in-laws or friends to accommodate his family in order to keep his son safe from being attacked. The RPD found that his failure to do so impugns his credibility that his son was targeted by the Sango idol worshippers. Ultimately the RPD found that the Appellant's evidence regarding his son being targeted was not credible.

The Appellant argues that the RPD's examination regarding the failure to relocate his family lacks transparency and deviates from the essence of the claim and that the RPD's expectations of the Appellant regarding the relocation of his family are faulty in that it infused its own values in the determination of reasonableness. I disagree.

The failure of the Appellant to reasonably explain why he did not include in his BOC form that his son was targeted by the Sango idol worshippers impugns his credibility that his son was targeted. If he had provided credible evidence that his son was targeted, his explanation that he did not take steps to relocate his family because the direct threat against his son was not imminent and because he lacked the means to support his family elsewhere in Nigeria may have been reasonable. However, the omission of the threat against his son, combined with the lack of relocation efforts, leads me to conclude that his son was not likely targeted at all. Documentary evidence - Letter from church

The RPD found that the letter from the Appellant's pastor establishes that the Appellant is Christian but that it is insufficient to prove that Sango worshippers targeted him in Nigeria. As a result, the RPD gave the document no weight.

The Appellant argues that this finding is patently flawed as the use of the term "insufficient"15 suggests that some weight is ascribed to the document, yet the RPD gave it no weight. I agree with the Appellant that the RPD's analysis of weight and sufficiency is not clear, but I agree with the finding of the RPD that the letter does not establish, on a balance of probabilities, that Sango worshippers targeted the Appellant in Nigeria.

The Federal Court in Magonza16 recognized the intersection between sufficiency of evidence, credibility, probative value, and weight and that the way in which these terms are utilized in decision writing can impact the intelligibility of reasons. The Court suggests that, when conducting a fact-finding analysis, it is helpful to consider as a convention that weight is a function of credibility and probative value.17

In this case, the letter from the pastor was found by the RPD to credibly establish that the Appellant is Christian. I agree with this finding. However, the letter does not address the factual question of whether the Appellant was or is targeted by Sango idol worshippers. A finding that the Appellant is Christian does not automatically make him a target of Sango idol worshippers. It is alleged by the Appellant that he was targeted because he is the first-born son of a Sango chief priest, not because of his Christianity (although this was the reason for his refusal of the position). The letter therefore has no probative value in relation to the issue of whether he was actually targeted and is given no weight. Once it is given no weight, then the letter will be insufficient on its own to establish, on a balance of probabilities, the fact in question, which is whether the Appellant was targeted by the Sango worshippers. I find that the RPD was correct in assigning no weight to the letter and in concluding that the Appellant had not established, on a balance of probabilities, that he is targeted to become a chief priest.

Due to the numerous inconsistencies, omissions, and contradictions which were not reasonably explained, and given that the documentary evidence did not support the Appellant's claim, the RPD concluded that the Appellant has failed to establish that he was targeted by Sango worshippers from 2011 until his departure from Nigeria in XXXX 2017. Despite the error I have identified regarding the consideration of the RIR, I find that the RPD was correct in its assessment of the Appellant's claim. The Appellant is not credible in his allegations and the documentary evidence does not assist the Appellant in establishing his claim.

I dismiss the appeal and confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.
